title: Market-Making Games
tagline: The trader interview's centerpiece — price a market, manage risk, and update as information arrives.

concept.analogy: It's like being asked to run a betting booth on a number nobody knows yet — say, 'how many windows are in this building?' You quote 'I'll buy your bet at 80, sell at 100.' People who think it's higher buy from you; people who think it's lower sell to you. Each trade leaks information about what others believe, and you must keep adjusting your booth's prices so you don't end up holding a hugely wrong position. That live tightrope is the market-making game.
paragraphs: Market-making games are the signature trading-interview exercise (especially at Jane Street, Optiver, SIG, IMC). The interviewer asks you to make a two-sided market — a bid and an ask — on some uncertain quantity: the sum of two dice, the number of countries in Africa, a fictional commodity, the price of a card. You quote, they trade against you, new information arrives, and you re-quote. They're grading your reasoning process, not whether you guess the number.

Four skills are tested. Calibration: is your market centered near a sensible expected value, and is your spread appropriately wide given your uncertainty? Bayesian updating: when the interviewer 'buys' or 'sells' (or reveals a hint), do you revise your market in the right direction and amount? Risk management: do you control the inventory you accumulate and avoid getting run over? Aggression: when you have a genuine edge, do you actually trade, rather than quoting so wide you never transact?

The core mechanic mirrors real market making (see the strategies lesson): your bid/ask straddle your fair-value estimate; the spread reflects your uncertainty and risk; and the fact that someone wants to trade against you is itself information (adverse selection / Bayesian updating) — if a smart counterparty keeps lifting your offer, your offer is probably too low.

These are learnable. Practice with a partner, narrate your EV and uncertainty out loud, update visibly when 'traded' against, and manage your running position. The Visualize tab's market-making game lets you feel the spread/inventory/adverse-selection trade-offs hands-on.
points: Make a two-sided market on an uncertain quantity; the interviewer trades against you and feeds info.
Graded on: calibration (center + spread), Bayesian updating, risk/inventory control, and aggression.
A counterparty's willingness to trade is information — update your market (adverse selection).
Center near EV; widen the spread when uncertain; tighten as you learn.
Narrate your reasoning out loud — the process is the score.
concept.keyIdea: A market-making game tests whether you can quote a calibrated two-sided market, update it Bayesially as you're traded against, and manage inventory — while being willing to trade on real edge. It's real market making, compressed into a conversation.

deepDive.intro: A concrete playbook for the game, and how each move maps to real trading.

steps.title: Anchor on expected value
steps.detail: First estimate the fair value (EV) of the quantity. For 'sum of two dice', EV = 7. For an unknown like 'flights in the air right now', do a quick Fermi estimate. Your market should be centered roughly here — quoting 5 @ 9 around a fair value of 7 (so bid 5, ask 9).

steps.title: Set spread by uncertainty and risk
steps.detail: The width reflects how unsure you are and how much you fear being picked off. Very unsure → wide market (protect yourself); confident → tighter (you'll trade more, capture more). Too wide and you never trade (failing 'aggression'); too tight and a knowledgeable interviewer picks you off (failing risk control). Start moderately wide, then tighten as you learn.

steps.title: Update when traded against
steps.detail: If the interviewer BUYS at your ask, that's evidence the true value is at least that high — shift your whole market UP (raise bid and ask). If they SELL at your bid, shift DOWN. The direction and size of your update should reflect how informed you think they are. Failing to update after being hit repeatedly is the classic mistake.

steps.title: Manage inventory
steps.detail: Track your position. If you keep getting lifted (selling, going short), you're accumulating risk in one direction — skew your market (lower both quotes) to encourage the offsetting trade and discourage more of the same, exactly like inventory skew in real market making. Don't let a runaway position build.

steps.title: Trade when you have edge
steps.detail: If you become confident the fair value is, say, 12 and someone offers to sell you at 9, take it — that's free EV. Interviewers want to see you act on edge, not just defend. Calibrated aggression (size up when confident, down when not) is a strong signal.

notes.title: Saying the right things
notes.detail: Narrate: 'My EV is about 7; I'm fairly uncertain so I'll make it 5 at 9. … You bought at 9 — that updates me upward, I'll move to 7 at 11. … I'm now short two lots, so I'll skew down to manage inventory.' This running commentary is exactly what's scored.

pitfalls: Not updating after being traded against — ignoring the information in the trade.
Quoting so wide you never transact (fails the 'will you trade on edge?' test).
Quoting too tight on a quantity you're very unsure about — easy to pick off.
Losing track of inventory and getting run over in one direction.
Going silent — failing to narrate your EV, uncertainty, and updates.

practice.intro: Practice these out loud as if a partner is trading against you. Use the Visualize tab to feel spread/inventory/adverse-selection live.

interviewQuestions.q: Make a market on the sum of two fair dice. The interviewer immediately buys from you at your ask. What do you do next?
a: Fair value (EV) of the sum is 7. I'm not very uncertain (the distribution is known and bounded 2–12, peaked at 7), so I can make a reasonably tight market — say 6 at 8 (bid 6, ask 8).

The interviewer buying at my ask of 8 is mild information that they think the value is ≥ 8 — but here the distribution is fully known, so I shouldn't over-update on their action alone (they may just be testing me). I'd note the information, perhaps nudge up slightly to 6.5 at 8.5 to manage the short inventory I just took on (I sold, so I'm short), and stay near EV 7. The key signals: I anchored on EV, sized my spread to my (low) uncertainty, acknowledged the trade as information, and managed inventory — without panicking on one trade in a known distribution.
followups: What if instead it's the sum of two dice but the interviewer secretly looked at one die? How does that change your spread?
How wide if it were the sum of 100 dice?

interviewQuestions.q: Make a market on a quantity you don't know — say, the number of piano tuners in Chicago. How do you approach it?
a: First Fermi-estimate the fair value: ~3M people in Chicago, maybe 1 in 20 households (avg ~2.5 people) has a piano that's tuned ~once/year → ~3M/2.5 = 1.2M households × (say) 5% with a piano ≈ 60,000 pianos/year of tunings; a tuner does maybe ~3/day × ~200 days ≈ 600/year, so ~60,000/600 ≈ ~100 tuners. (The classic estimate lands around 50–125.)

Because I'm genuinely uncertain, I quote a WIDE market around ~100 — say 60 at 160. Then I update on any information: if the interviewer aggressively buys at 160, the true value is probably higher and I shift up and maybe widen; if they sell at 60, I shift down. I narrate the estimate, keep the spread honest to my uncertainty, update on their trades, and watch my inventory. Wide-but-centered with disciplined updating beats a falsely precise tight quote.

interviewQuestions.q: The interviewer says 'make me a market on X' (e.g., the sum of two dice). What does that mean and how do you respond well?
a: 'Make a market' means quote a two-sided price: a bid (where you'll buy) and an ask (where you'll sell), around your estimate of fair value, with a spread that reflects your uncertainty. The interviewer can then 'trade' against you (buy at your ask or sell at your bid), and may keep trading or reveal information, watching how you update. They're testing your estimation, your sizing of uncertainty (spread width), and your discipline when traded against (adverse selection).

Respond well by: (1) estimating fair value out loud (for two dice, E[sum] = 7); (2) quoting a spread around it that's wide enough to protect against being picked off but tight enough to be competitive (e.g., '6 at 8' — bid 6, ask 8); (3) updating after each trade — if they keep buying at your ask, your fair value is probably too low, so raise your market; (4) managing 'inventory' and not getting repeatedly run over. The cardinal rule: when someone trades against you, assume they might know something and adjust — don't stubbornly hold a market that keeps getting hit on one side.
followups: If I keep lifting your offer, what do you do?
How wide should your spread be and why?

problems.title: Make and manage a market on two dice
problems.statement: Interviewer: 'I'll roll two fair dice; make me a market on their sum.' (a) State fair value and a reasonable quote. (b) The interviewer BUYS from you at your ask, then buys again. How should you update your market and why? (c) Suppose instead they reveal one die already shows a 6 — re-quote. Walk through your reasoning as you would out loud.
problems.hint: E[sum]=7. Spread reflects uncertainty/risk. Repeated one-sided trading is information. Conditioning on a die=6 shifts fair value.
problems.tests: Market-making intuition: fair value, spread, updating, conditioning.

approach: (a) Fair value: E[sum of two dice] = 7. Quote a spread around it, e.g., '6 at 8' (I buy at 6, sell at 8). Width reflects that the sum ranges 2–12 with stdev ≈ 2.4, and that the interviewer may be informed; tighter (e.g., 6.5 at 7.5) is more competitive but riskier if they know something.

(b) They buy at my ask (8), then buy again: persistent one-sided buying is information that my market is too low (they think fair value > 8, or they have an edge). I should raise my whole market — e.g., move to '8 at 10' — and consider widening the spread to protect against adverse selection. I also now hold short 'inventory' (I sold twice), so I lean my quotes up to discourage selling more and encourage buying back. The mistake to avoid is leaving my offer at 8 and getting repeatedly picked off.

(c) If one die is revealed as 6, the sum = 6 + (other die), and E[other die] = 3.5, so fair value updates to 6 + 3.5 = 9.5, with the sum now ranging 7–12 (tighter, lower variance). I'd re-quote around 9.5, e.g., '9 at 10', narrower than before because conditioning on the 6 reduced my uncertainty. This shows the two core skills: compute the conditional expected value when information arrives, and adjust both the center (fair value) and the width (spread) of your market accordingly — exactly what a real market maker does as the book and flow reveal information.

problems.title: How wide should your market be?
problems.statement: You're asked to make a market on a quantity you estimate at fair value 50, but you're quite uncertain (your own estimate could be off by ±10), and the interviewer is clearly better-informed than you. Discuss how you choose your spread width, how being traded against changes your estimate, and the failure mode of quoting too tight against an informed counterparty.
problems.hint: Spread should scale with your uncertainty AND the counterparty's information advantage; adverse selection punishes tight quotes.
problems.tests: Spread-setting under uncertainty and adverse selection.

approach: Spread width should scale with two things: your own uncertainty about fair value (±10 here is large, so a wider spread), and the information asymmetry — if the counterparty is better-informed, every trade they do is likely adverse to you, so you must widen further to be compensated for getting picked off. A reasonable quote might be something like '44 at 56' (a 12-wide market around 50), not '49 at 51'.

Updating: because the counterparty is informed, treat any trade as a signal. If they buy from you, fair value is probably higher than you thought — raise your market; if they sell, lower it. You're essentially doing Bayesian updating on their actions, and you should move quickly when traded against rather than stubbornly defending a level.

Failure mode of quoting too tight: against an informed trader, a narrow spread means they only trade when they have an edge over you, so you systematically lose the spread to adverse selection — you get bought from right before the value rises and sold to right before it falls ('picked off'). The classic beginner mistake in these games is quoting a tight, confident market to look smart, then getting run over on one side. The disciplined play is to size your spread to your uncertainty and the toxicity of the flow, widen and skew when repeatedly traded on one side, and accept that a wider market that survives beats a tight one that bleeds.
